en: The *Saptajñāna-sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the lay devotee Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi country during the Wu dynasty.
Thus have I heard: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. The Buddha addressed the monks:
The bhikṣus replied,
“We shall receive the instruction and listen to the Buddha.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“There are seven qualities by which a disciple on the path dwells in peace, comfort, and joy in the present life, practicing with diligence and developing the contemplation of phenomena until they reach their ultimate exhaustion.
What are these seven qualities?
"First, knowledge of the Dharma; second, knowledge of the meaning; third, knowledge of the time; fourth, knowledge of moderation; fifth, self-knowledge; sixth, knowledge of the assembly;
seventh, knowledge of individuals. O Bhikṣus!"
What is meant by "knowing the Dharma"?
It refers to being able to understand the twelve divisions of the scriptures:

first, prose; second, verse; third, exposition; fourth, stanzas; fifth, parables; sixth, accounts of past lives; seventh, explanations of events; eighth, biographies of births; ninth, extensive treatises; tenth, spontaneous teachings; eleventh, practices; and twelfth, chapters and sections. This is what is meant by knowing the Dharma.
Not understanding the twelve divisions of the scriptures is called not knowing the Dharma.
What is meant by "knowing the meaning"?
To fully comprehend the meaning of each and every scripture and teaching that has been spoken—this is what is meant by knowing the meaning.
To fail to understand and comprehend what has been taught in various instances is to be ignorant of its meaning.
What is meant by "knowing the proper time"?

It means knowing that at this time one should contemplate the thought of cessation (*śānti*), that at this time one should not contemplate the thought of receiving and practicing [precepts], and that at this time one should contemplate the thought of careful protection; this is called knowing the proper time.
To act without understanding the appropriateness of the time is called "not knowing the time.
What is meant by "knowing moderation"?

Being able to consume food and drink in small amounts so that excrement and urine are properly digested; being able to regulate one's going out and coming in, sitting and rising, and walking; and ensuring that sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent are all conducted with brevity and economy—this is called knowing moderation.
To fail to restrain and examine oneself is to lack knowledge of moderation. What is meant by "knowing oneself"? It means knowing for oneself the extent of one's own physical and mental aging;

knowing what one believes and what one guards against; what one has heard and what one has practiced in giving; what one possesses of wisdom and what one understands; and the depth or shallowness, the intensity or mildness of every state one reaches and enters—knowing each of these matters for oneself is what is meant by "knowing oneself."
Not knowing the extent to which one’s own mind has entered [the assembly] is called "not knowing oneself.
What is meant by "knowing the assembly"?

It is being able to recognize whether that assembly consists of nobles, householders, brahmins, or ascetics; and whether, at any given time, it is appropriate to sit or stand, or appropriate to speak or remain silent—knowing what is appropriate for the occasion is what is meant by "knowing the assembly."
Not knowing the characteristics of that assembly and what is appropriate for the occasion constitutes not knowing the assembly.
What is meant by "knowing people"?

Suppose there are two persons: one who believes in the Way and one who does not believe in the Way. The one who believes in the Way is worthy of praise, while the one who does not believe is not worthy of praise.
There are two classes of those who believe in the Way:
one class frequently visits the site of practice and delights in the śramaṇas; the other class does not frequently visit the site of practice and regards the śramaṇas with intellectual skepticism.
Those who visit frequently are worthy of praise; those who do not visit frequently are not worthy of praise.
There are two types of people who frequently visit the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*):
one who loves and respects the śramaṇas, and one who does not love or respect the śramaṇas.
The one who loves and respects them is worthy of praise; the one who does not love or respect them is not worthy of praise.
There are two classes of those who practice love and respect:
those who are personally acquainted with śramaṇas, and those who are not personally acquainted with śramaṇas.
Those who are personally acquainted may be praised; those who are not personally acquainted cannot be praised.
There are two types of those who associate with others:
one person delights in inquiring about the scriptures and the Dharma, while another does not delight in inquiring about the scriptures and the Dharma.
The one who delights in inquiry may be praised; the one who does not delight in inquiry is not praised.
There are two types of those who love to inquire:
one listens with the ear cocked, and the other does not listen with the ear cocked.
Those who listen with the ear cocked may be praised; those who do not listen with the ear cocked cannot be praised.
Listening with attentive ears involves two types of people:
one who hears the Dharma and upholds it, and one who hears the Dharma but does not uphold it.
The one who hears the Dharma and upholds it may be praised; the one who does not uphold it cannot be praised.
There are two types of those who uphold [the teaching]:
one who hears it and contemplates its meaning, and one who hears it but does not contemplate its meaning.
He who hears it and contemplates its meaning is worthy of praise; he who hears it but does not contemplate its meaning is not worthy of praise.
There are two types of people who hear the Dharma and contemplate its meaning:

one person understands the meaning according to the sūtra and receives the Dharma by establishing themselves in accordance with the Dharma; the other person does not understand the meaning according to the sūtra and does not receive the Dharma by establishing themselves in accordance with the Dharma.
One who explains the meaning of the sūtras in accordance with the sūtras is worthy of praise; one who explains the meaning of the sūtras contrary to the sūtras is not worthy of praise.
There are two types of those who explain the meaning of the sūtras in accordance with the sūtras:

the first person merely brings peace to themselves, but does not bring peace to others, does not bring much peace to people, does not take pity on the world, and does not benefit the realm of men; the second person is able to bring peace to themselves and also brings peace to others, bringing much peace to the world, taking pity on the world, and benefiting and bringing tranquility to devas and humans.

“O bhikṣus, you should distinguish them: he who establishes himself in peace, is able to establish others in peace, brings peace to many in the world, and out of compassion for the world seeks the benefit and tranquility of all beings—such a person is the most excellent, the eldest, the most venerable, and the most supreme.”
For example, it is like cow’s milk turning into curd, curd into butter, and butter into clarified butter (*ghṛta*); among these, clarified butter is supreme.

In the same way, such a person is the most excellent among men; they possess superior conduct, honored conduct, and the most exalted conduct; they are the most victorious, the highest, and unsurpassed in their vows.
"O bhikṣus!

Those who are able to see two kinds of people—regarding them as wise and superior, and being able to distinguish that 'this person is virtuous' and 'this person is excellent'—these are called those who know men."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this, they all received it with joy.
The Sūtra on the Seven Knowledges Spoken by the Buddha.
